source_text: Unde quamvis omnia, quae contra nos edidisti, scripta ad unum finem properent, videlicet ut naturalia mala esse persuadeas et aut diabolum hominum aut Deum criminum conditorem, tamen puto aliquid procedere ad studium brevitatis, si ea potissimum argumenta, quibus totam opinionem tuam tueri te, cum obumbraris, putas, de diversis in unum partibus congregavero eaque prius admota expositione iuvero, ut, quid conentur, appareat, post vero non sparsa, sed collecta, non involuta, sed explicata proruero.
pass_a_gloss: Whence although all things which you have edited against us hasten to one end, namely that you persuade natural things to be evils and either the devil the founder of humans or God of crimes, nevertheless I think something proceeds to the study of brevity if I gather into one from diverse parts those arguments especially by which you think, when you are overshadowed, to guard your whole opinion, and those first I will help by an exposition moved, that what they attempt may appear, afterward not scattered but collected, not wrapped but explained I will overthrow.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Everything you have published against us rushes toward one goal: persuading us that natural things are evil and that either the devil creates humans or God creates crimes. Still, I think brevity will gain something if I gather from different places into one account the chief arguments with which, when you wrap yourself in obscurity, you think you defend your whole opinion. I will first help them by an explanation, making clear what they attempt; then I will overthrow them, gathered rather than scattered, unfolded rather than tangled.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Augustine's quoted claim that the unbaptized remain under the devil; keep the personal devil, not 'evil'.
rejected: under Satan (name not in the Latin here)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
